children.text: T1: Solenoid and loop

A closed circular loop of radius \(r\) consists of an ideal battery of electromotive force \(\mathcal E\) and a wire of resistance \(R\). A long thin air-core solenoid is aligned with the axis of the loop (\(z\)-axis). Its length is \(\ell\gg r\), cross-sectional area is \(A\) (\(\sqrt A\ll r\)), and the number of turns is \(N\). The solenoid is powered by a constant current \(I\) provided by an ideal current source. The directions of the currents in the solenoid and in the loop are the same (clockwise in the figure).

nodes.alt: Original setup: a long thin solenoid with head O_1 and tail O_2, length ell and N turns, approaches a coaxial circular loop of radius r powered by a battery.

children.text: a

Find the force \(F_1\) acting on the solenoid when its head \(O_1\) is positioned in the loop centre \(O\). What is the force \(F_2\) acting on the solenoid when its tail \(O_2\) is located in the centre of the loop?
b

Suppose now that the solenoid is moving slowly with a constant velocity \(v\) along the \(z\)-axis starting far away from the loop, going past its centre, and proceeding further to the right in the positive \(z\)-direction. Plot the current \(J\) flowing in the loop as a function of time. Highlight important features and values on the graph. The velocity \(v\) is so small that self-inductance of the loop can be neglected.

statement.text:
T1: Solenoid and loop
A closed circular loop of radius \(r\) consists of an ideal battery of electromotive force \(\mathcal E\) and a wire of resistance \(R\). A long thin air-core solenoid is aligned with the axis of the loop (\(z\)-axis). Its length is \(\ell\gg r\), cross-sectional area is \(A\) (\(\sqrt A\ll r\)), and the number of turns is \(N\). The solenoid is powered by a constant current \(I\) provided by an ideal current source. The directions of the currents in the solenoid and in the loop are the same (clockwise in the figure).

a
Find the force \(F_1\) acting on the solenoid when its head \(O_1\) is positioned in the loop centre \(O\). What is the force \(F_2\) acting on the solenoid when its tail \(O_2\) is located in the centre of the loop?
b
Suppose now that the solenoid is moving slowly with a constant velocity \(v\) along the \(z\)-axis starting far away from the loop, going past its centre, and proceeding further to the right in the positive \(z\)-direction. Plot the current \(J\) flowing in the loop as a function of time. Highlight important features and values on the graph. The velocity \(v\) is so small that self-inductance of the loop can be neglected.

children.text: T1: Solenoid and loop
a. Solution I: force on the loop

The stationary loop carries current \(J=\mathcal E/R\). Newton's third law gives the force on the solenoid as the opposite of the force on the loop. A long, thin solenoid can be represented externally by a north pole at \(O_1\) and a south pole at \(O_2\). Each pole has flux magnitude equal to the flux through a cross-section of the solenoid.
\[\Phi=B_{\rm in}A=\mu_0\frac{NI}{\ell}A.\]
With \(O_1=O\), the far pole is negligible. The near pole produces an outward radial field of magnitude
\[B(r)=\frac{\Phi}{4\pi r^2}=\frac{\mu_0NIA}{4\pi\ell r^2}.\]
Summing \(J\,d\mathbf l\times\mathbf B\) around the loop gives a force in the negative \(z\)-direction. The solenoid experiences the opposite force.
\[F_1=\frac{\mathcal E}{R}\,2\pi r\,B(r)=\frac{\mu_0NIA\mathcal E}{2\ell Rr},\qquad \mathbf F_1=F_1\mathbf e_z,\qquad \mathbf F_2=-F_1\mathbf e_z.\]

When \(O_2=O\), the radial field reverses, hence so does the force. The source also permits a hemisphere construction using half the internal field flux and half the spherical area. It gives the same radial field.
a. Solution II: force on a magnetic pole
The total magnetic moment is \(m=NIA\). Writing this as \(Q_m\ell\) gives the pole strength. The field at the centre of the battery-powered loop follows from the Biot-Savart law.
\[Q_m=\frac{NIA}{\ell}=\frac{\Phi}{\mu_0},\qquad B_{\rm loop}(0)=\frac{\mu_0J}{2r}=\frac{\mu_0\mathcal E}{2Rr},\qquad F_1=Q_mB_{\rm loop}(0).\]

The north pole is pushed in the positive \(z\)-direction and the south pole in the negative direction. The pole analogy can also be justified by virtual work on the field energy: electric and magnetic energy densities are \(\varepsilon_0E^2/2\) and \(B^2/(2\mu_0)\), respectively. The substitutions \(\varepsilon_0^{-1}\leftrightarrow\mu_0\), \(E\leftrightarrow B\) and \(Q\leftrightarrow Q_m\) give
\[F_E=\frac{Q^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r^2}\quad\longleftrightarrow\quad F_B=\frac{\mu_0Q_m^2}{4\pi r^2},\qquad Q=\varepsilon_0\Psi\quad\longleftrightarrow\quad Q_m=\frac{\Phi}{\mu_0}.\]
a. Solution III: flux through the side

The loop field enters the near end of the solenoid with flux \(\Phi_{\rm in}=\mu_0\mathcal E A/(2Rr)\). Almost no flux escapes through the distant end, so it leaves through the side. For a circular turn with perimeter \(c=2\sqrt{\pi A}\), let \(B_i\) be the radial component at that turn. Its axial force is \(F_i=cIB_i\). Axial field components produce radial forces that cancel by symmetry.
\[F_1=I\frac N\ell\sum_i c\frac\ell N B_i=I\frac N\ell\Phi_{\rm in}=\frac{\mu_0\mathcal E ANI}{2Rr\ell}.\]
a. Solution IV: integrate magnetic dipoles
A short segment has dipole moment \(d\mathbf m=IAN\,dz\,\mathbf e_z/\ell\). Its axial force is \(dm\,dB_{\rm loop}/dz\). Thus
\[B_{\rm loop}(z)=\frac{\mu_0\mathcal E}{2R}\frac{r^2}{(z^2+r^2)^{3/2}},\qquad F_1=\frac{IAN}{\ell}\left[B_{\rm loop}(0)-B_{\rm loop}(-\ell)\right].\]
\[F_1=\frac{\mu_0\mathcal E ANI r^2}{2R\ell}\left[\frac1{r^3}-\frac1{(\ell^2+r^2)^{3/2}}\right]\simeq\frac{\mu_0\mathcal E ANI}{2\ell Rr}.\]

A related construction uses Gauss's law for the magnetic field to obtain the radial flux through each segment from the change in axial field, then integrates the Lorentz force. It gives the same result.
a. Solution V: energy and the sources

Move the solenoid a small distance \(\delta z\) in the positive direction while an external force balances the magnetic force. The system includes its power supplies. The field energy alone is not the total energy.
\[-F_1\delta z=\delta E_{\rm total}=\delta E_{\rm field}+\delta E_{\rm sources}.\]
For this virtual displacement, replace the battery by a source holding \(J=\mathcal E/R\) constant. Only the mutual-inductance term changes.
\[E_{\rm field}=\frac12L_1I^2+\frac12L_2J^2+L_{12}IJ,\qquad \delta E_{\rm field}=IJ\,\delta L_{12}.\]
\[V_{\rm ind}^{\rm loop}=-I\frac{\delta L_{12}}{\delta t},\qquad V_{\rm ind}^{\rm solenoid}=-J\frac{\delta L_{12}}{\delta t},\qquad \delta E_{\rm sources}=-2IJ\,\delta L_{12}.\]
Consequently \(\delta E_{\rm total}=-\delta E_{\rm field}\) and \(F_1\delta z=IJ\,\delta L_{12}\). Moving a segment from the tail to the head changes the linked flux by
\[J\,\delta L_{21}=B_{\rm loop}(0)A\frac N\ell\delta z,\qquad L_{21}=L_{12},\qquad F_1=\frac{\mu_0\mathcal E NAI}{2\ell Rr}.\]

With the tail at the centre, mutual inductance decreases and the force reverses. Without sources, superconducting circuits would conserve flux and their currents would change. Treating their field energy as if both currents were fixed gives the wrong sign.

The field-energy change can alternatively be evaluated by transferring a segment \(\delta z\) from tail to head, with \(\ell\gg\delta z\gg\sqrt A\). The internal solenoid field is \(B_{\rm sol}=\mu_0NI/\ell\), giving
\[\delta E_{\rm field}=\frac{A\delta z}{2\mu_0}\left[(B_{\rm loop}(0)+B_{\rm sol})^2-B_{\rm loop}(0)^2-B_{\rm sol}^2\right].\]

A third version uses the potential energy \(-\mathbf m\cdot\mathbf B\) of the transferred turns. This effective potential already includes the source-energy sign. The solenoid's own field is the same at both ends and cancels, while the distant loop field is negligible.
\[\delta E_{\rm pot}=-\frac{IAN\delta z}{\ell}\frac{\mu_0\mathcal E}{2Rr},\qquad F_1=-\frac{\delta E_{\rm pot}}{\delta z}.\]
b. Current and graph
Take \(t=0\) when the solenoid's centre passes \(O\). Then \(z_1=vt+\ell/2\) and \(z_2=vt-\ell/2\). Negligible self-inductance gives
\[J(t)=\frac{\mathcal E+V_{\rm ind}(t)}{R}.\]
Solution I uses the solid angles subtended by the loop at the two poles. The flux and its time derivative are
\[\Phi_{\rm loop}=\frac{\mu_0NIA}{2\ell}\left[\frac{z_1}{\sqrt{z_1^2+r^2}}-\frac{z_2}{\sqrt{z_2^2+r^2}}\right],\]
\[V_{\rm ind}=-\frac{d\Phi_{\rm loop}}{dt}=-\frac{v\mu_0NIA}{2\ell}\left[\frac{r^2}{(z_1^2+r^2)^{3/2}}-\frac{r^2}{(z_2^2+r^2)^{3/2}}\right].\]
Solution II uses reciprocity, \(L_{12}=L_{21}\). Temporarily hold a test loop current \(J_0\) fixed. Transferring a segment from tail to head gives
\[J_0\,dL_{21}=v\,dt\,\frac{NA}{\ell}\left[B_{\rm loop}(z_1)-B_{\rm loop}(z_2)\right],\qquad V_{\rm ind}=-I\frac{dL_{12}}{dt}.\]

Substituting the loop field gives the same expression. Transcription note: the source's intermediate prose drops the minus sign in \(V_{\rm ind}=I\dot L_{12}\) and labels a flux derivative with the reciprocal indices. The final negative derivative and the plotted current fix the intended sign and convention.

The deviation \(J-\mathcal E/R\) is odd in time. Initially the increasing flux reduces the current. Later the decreasing flux increases it. Far away, the solenoid field behaves as a dipole field, so \(V_{\rm ind}\) decays as \(|t|^{-4}\). Near the centre the deviation is small and approximately linear in \(t\). The dip and peak occur close to \(-\ell/(2v)\) and \(+\ell/(2v)\), with widths of order \(r/v\) and a separation approximately \(\ell/v\).
\[J_{\min}\simeq\frac{\mathcal E}{R}-\frac{v\mu_0NIA}{2Rr\ell},\qquad J_{\max}\simeq\frac{\mathcal E}{R}+\frac{v\mu_0NIA}{2Rr\ell}.\]

These extrema use \(\ell\gg r\), neglecting the other pole. The curve is smooth and locally quadratic about each extremum. The source's summary table abbreviates this quadratic behaviour without writing the nonzero extremal offset. The full formula above supplies that offset.

nodes.alt: Original current graph for ell equal to 5r: baseline E/R, a smooth dip near minus ell/(2v), a peak near plus ell/(2v), and return to the same baseline. Both extrema and the time scales ell/v and r/v are labelled.
